title: Special factoring patterns and vertex form
subtitle: Equivalent expressions · 13 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **13 of the official questions in Equivalent expressions are this one** — 4 Easy, 5 Medium, 4 Hard.
Most versions sit at the Medium tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- You see a trinomial whose first and last terms are perfect squares, a difference of two squares, a degree-4 expression with only even powers (a quadratic in x²), or choices written as (x ± h)² ± k.
- The question asks which is a factor or which is equivalent.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Check for a perfect square a² ± 2ab + b², a difference of squares a² − b², or substitute u = x² to turn a quartic into an ordinary quadratic.
- 2) For vertex-form choices, halve the x-coefficient to get h, square it, and adjust the constant so it still matches.
- 3) Expand the choice you pick to confirm the middle term.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Its x-intercepts give the roots, and a root r means (x − r) is a factor.
For vertex form, click the vertex and read (h, k) directly.
This is often the fastest route.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You get the sign of h wrong in vertex form ((x − 3)² gives a vertex at x = +3).
Or you pick factor pairs of the constant that multiply correctly but don't add to the middle coefficient, or forget to factor the coefficients themselves (the 9 in 9x²).

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You get the sign of h wrong in vertex form ((x − 3)² gives a vertex at x = +3).
Or you pick factor pairs of the constant that multiply correctly but don't add to the middle coefficient, or forget to factor the coefficients themselves (the 9 in 9x²).
